FinFlow account-takeover investigation

184,432 payments and 72,621 login sessions, April 1 – June 30 2026. Red marks confirmed fraud (txn_fraud_label).

I let Claude roam free, inside three guardrails

Claude reads the files, runs the code and builds whole sections on its own. I don't hold its hand prompt by prompt. The guardrails are what make that safe.

Guardrail 1

CLAUDE.md = how I like to work

Claude reads it at the start of every session. It's nearly the same in every project I have, just tweaked a bit for each one:

  • Keep it succinct and precise. No filler, no restating what was just discussed.
  • Attach validation to anything you output.
  • Confirm before anything hard to reverse or visible outside this machine.

README.md = what the project is

The goal, the data and its traps. Claude reads this too. Keeping the two apart means the rules for how we work don't get buried in project facts.

  • A take-home case study for a Risk Data Scientist interview at BILL.
  • The data: two CSVs, logins (~72k) and payments (~184k), joined on session_id. 90 days from April 1, 2026, all times in UTC.
  • Don't let the model see the future. That's data leakage.
Guardrail 2

git must have

Nothing reaches prod without a human review. Claude works on a branch and opens a PR. I read the PR and I'm the one who merges. It never pushes on its own. From my research repo's CLAUDE.md:

  • Never push without explicit confirmation for that push, even if a previous push in the same session was approved.
  • Keep commits scoped to one method/module at a time.

Every step is a commit, so any wrong turn is one revert away. That's what makes it cheap to let Claude try things.

Guardrail 3

Plan mode is your best friend

Claude writes the plan before touching anything. I read it line by line and push back before any code exists. More on this below.

Getting the most out of plan mode

Before Claude touches a file, it writes out what it's going to do: which files, what changes, and how it'll check its work. Nothing gets built until I approve it. That makes the plan the cheapest place to catch a mistake. A wrong idea costs one sentence to fix in the plan, and an hour once it's code.

What I look for when I read a plan
  • Did it understand what I actually asked, or a nearby version of it?
  • Is it building something I don't need?
  • Is there a step where it checks its own work?
  • Is there anything I'd have to defend that I don't understand yet?
How I actually use it
  • Only for big calls, like setting up a method or planning a talk. Small stuff gets a one-line prompt.
  • I almost never approve the first plan. I turn it down and keep adding notes until it's right.
  • I edit the plan file myself. It's a shared doc, not a contract Claude hands me.
  • I bring outside material in, like notes from other sessions, and ask what it changes.

Tips

  • Write a precise prompt. Clean spelling and grammar, short, no fuzzy words. A vague ask gets a vague plan.
  • Spend the time on details up front. Every minute of back and forth on the plan saves more later in rework.
  • Have a picture of the end product. If you don't have one yet, plan mode is where you build it. Go back and forth with Claude until you can describe what "done" looks like.
  • Put tests in the plan. Where it fits, write the check first and build to it. Here that meant asserts on every join and a harness that runs every code block on this dashboard against the real CSVs (80/80 values match). This repo has no formal unit-test suite, though.
  • Pick the model for the job. In my experience Fable is better at planning and Opus is better at building. That's just my impression, I haven't measured it.
  • Use skills to give planning more structure. Skill packs like Superpowers add a brainstorm step before the plan and test-first habits during the build. They push you through the same steps every time.

Other habits

Mostly from this case study, so you can check them in the other tabs. The last one is how I usually work, but I skipped it here.

I make the design calls, Claude does the work. Swapping a plain foreign-login count for "foreign and new for that user" was my call. Claude built it, and the customer score split into two clean groups: 100 customers at zero, five at four.
Claude as a tutor and adversary. I ask Claude for its suggestions and thoughts. It challenges me and teaches me something new.
Saying no to extra work. xgboost was installed, but I started with logistic regression and a small tree. A coefficient is easier to defend than a boosted ensemble.
Check it a second way. Every number that could reach a slide got recomputed another way. I also had a harness run every code block on this page against the real CSVs: 80 of 80 values match.
Checking by reading. Most of my catches come from something not adding up. "Isn't there 2 break-ins?" showed June wasn't a break-in at all. "How could FinFlow have known on 22 April?" cut a headline from $5.20M to $2.52M.
Checking with a fresh Claude session. A new session hasn't seen the work, so it doesn't share the first one's blind spots. I open one, have it review what the first one made, and bring the findings back to compare.
Tests are part of the build. I usually have Claude write unit tests and doctests (small examples inside the code that run as tests) as it builds, not after. If a change breaks something, the tests catch it before I do. This take-home had a 4-hour cap, so I skipped them here.

Evidence & validation — how these totals are computed
import pandas as pd

txn = pd.read_csv("finflow_case_study_data/transactions.csv", parse_dates=["txn_ts"])

# The four tiles above, for whichever org is selected
per_org = (txn.groupby("org_id")
              .agg(payments=("txn_id", "size"),
                   volume=("amount", "sum"),
                   fraud=("txn_fraud_label", "sum")))
per_org["impacted"] = (txn[txn.txn_fraud_label].groupby("org_id").amount.sum()
                          .reindex(per_org.index).fillna(0))

per_org[per_org.fraud > 0].sort_values("fraud", ascending=False)
#           payments      volume  fraud   impacted
# org_0001       848   3,391,416    335  1,861,728
# org_0101       262   1,557,592    130  1,097,540
# org_0100      7329  25,024,495    108  2,103,788
# org_0017      1365   4,530,794     52    493,395
# org_0012      3499  10,840,285     33    303,921

# Note org_0100 lost MORE money than org_0001 -- and never reported it.
# The org that phoned FinFlow is not the worst-hit one.

5 of 110 organizations were touched; 105 were never hit. The How far it reaches tab establishes that boundary without using the fraud label.

How these two devices were found

Nothing here was assumed — the device list falls out of the data.

Evidence & validation
import pandas as pd

txn = pd.read_csv("finflow_case_study_data/transactions.csv", parse_dates=["txn_ts"])
log = pd.read_csv("finflow_case_study_data/logins.csv",       parse_dates=["login_ts"])

# A session is an "attack" session if it moved money that was later
# adjudicated fraud. This is the ONLY place the label is used.
fraud_sessions = set(txn.loc[txn.txn_fraud_label, "session_id"])
log["attack"] = log.session_id.isin(fraud_sessions)

# The devices those sessions ran on -- found, not assumed.
ATTACKER_DEVICES = sorted(log.loc[log.attack, "device_id"].unique())
log["att_dev"] = log.device_id.isin(ATTACKER_DEVICES)

atk   = log[log.attack]                   # 122 sessions that got in and moved money
recon = log[log.att_dev & ~log.attack]    #  46 sessions that were blocked
norm  = log[~log.att_dev]                 # 72,453 sessions on every other device

ATTACKER_DEVICES
# ['d_5019b1fc56a9', 'd_93bba37589da']      <- 2 of 728 devices

log.loc[log.att_dev, "user_id"].nunique()   # 5   (all seat _01)
log.loc[log.att_dev, "org_id"].nunique()    # 5   (of 110)
log.attack.sum()                            # 122 got in
(log.att_dev & ~log.attack).sum()           # 46  blocked

Attack sessions don't look like normal sessions

Share of sessions with each property. "Attack" = the 122 sessions that moved fraudulent money. "Normal" = all 72,453 sessions on every other device.
Excluded on purpose: "login succeeded" and "MFA failed". An attack session is defined as one that moved money, so it had to have logged in — those rows would restate the definition, not measure anything.

How far it spread

Five customers of 110, five user accounts of 520, 362 fake payees, $5.86M. The boundary holds without ever reading the fraud label — the working for that is on the What to build tab, where those same checks become the proposed features.

Evidence & validation — the counter this chart draws
# The line is one number, computed on every login attempt: how many failed MFA
# challenges this account racked up in the trailing 60 minutes.
log = log.sort_values(["user_id", "login_ts"])
log["failed"] = log.mfa_result.eq("failed")
log["burst"]  = (log.set_index("login_ts").groupby("user_id")
                    .failed.rolling("60min").sum().to_numpy())

# When would a threshold of 3 first fire on each account?
log[log.burst >= 3].groupby("user_id").login_ts.min()

# u_0001_01  2026-04-22 20:23   <- 102 min BEFORE its first fraudulent payment
# u_0012_01  2026-04-24 06:21   <-  19 min before
# u_0017_01  2026-04-23 04:58   <- 137 min AFTER  (money had already moved)
# u_0100_01  2026-04-24 03:27   <-  86 min after
# u_0101_01  2026-04-23 07:50   <- 331 min after

# Only two of the five are pre-empted outright. The rule still cuts off the bulk
# of the money on the other three, because most payments came later -- which is
# why the headline is 95.7% of dollars and not 100% of payments.

# The two accounts here with no fraud are the honest controls:
#   u_0008_01  10 failures in 90 days, worst hour 2  -- closest a real user gets

Reach in time: three orgs were robbed twice

Wave 2 is a strict subset of wave 1 — the same victims, the same two devices, two months later.

This is a remediation failure, not a second incident. FinFlow was told in April, ops reviewed 77% of the April fraud — and the same two fingerprints walked back in on 26 June and took another $2.52M. org_0012 and org_0017 were never hit again; whether that is successful remediation or the attacker simply not returning, this data cannot say.

Evidence & validation
f  = txn[txn.txn_fraud_label]
w1 = f[f.txn_ts <  "2026-05-01"]     # 383 payments, $3,340,332
w2 = f[f.txn_ts >= "2026-05-01"]     # 275 payments, $2,520,040

set(w1.org_id)                       # 5 orgs
set(w2.org_id)                       # 3 orgs
set(w2.org_id) <= set(w1.org_id)     # True -- a strict subset

# Wave 2 is not new victims. It is the same orgs, hit again by the same
# two device fingerprints, two months after the first report.

Two layers, and you want a control on each

Every fraudulent payment here crossed two separate lines. First they took over an account. Then they moved money out of it. Those are different problems with different signals, and the four controls below split between them.

Layer 1 — getting into the account Layer 2 — moving the money out
What happened Two device fingerprints hammered MFA on five admin accounts from rotating countries and VPNs until a challenge passed. All five are seat _01. Each hijacked account set up payees the customer had never paid, mostly on foreign banks with fresh bank details, then pushed wires.
Signals it leaves 3+ failed MFA in an hour; the same device at a second customer; a country new for that user; impossible travel. First-ever payment to a payee; new bank account; foreign vendor bank; wire rail; approval bypassed.
Present on 658 of 658 fraudulent payments came from one of the two attacker devices; 636 came after an MFA burst on that account. 658 of 658 went to a payee with no prior clean payment; 592 were flagged new bank account, 652 had a foreign bank, 574 were wires.
Controls below MFA lockout · cross-customer containment Hold the first payment to a payee · the review-queue model, which reads both

All 658 payments crossed both lines, which is why each layer reaches nearly everything on its own. Those two near-total numbers are not evidence that one layer is enough. They are two independent shots at the same campaign. Take one control from each column, because the layers fail differently: an attacker who logs in with valid stolen credentials leaves no Layer 1 trace at all, and one who hijacks a payee the customer already pays — changing its bank details rather than adding a payee — leaves no Layer 2 trace. Both of those are flagged as live gaps further down this tab.

Four things, ranked by what they would have saved

Each control is replayed against the real timeline: it only gets credit for fraud that happened after the moment it would have fired. The bar shows the share of the $5.86M it prevents. This is the case for each control and what it costs — not how to build it.
Biggest is not the same as first, and these do not add up. The two at the top prevent the most but carry real friction or real build cost, and they overlap heavily — the percentages are each control measured alone, so do not sum them. Cross-customer containment prevents less on paper and adds nothing on top of the MFA lockout, yet it is the cheapest thing here and the only one that does not depend on FinFlow having noticed anything in time.

The MFA lockout carries almost all of this on its own — 95.7% of the loss ($5.61M of $5.86M), with no model. Adding cross-customer containment on top prevents no additional dollars at all: the lockout already trips before the June wave, so containment reaches nothing the lockout has not reached. The 22 payments ($251,753) the lockout misses came from sessions entered before any MFA burst, and containment cannot reach those either.

That is not an argument against containment. It is an argument about why you build it. Containment is worth shipping because it is the only control here that does not depend on FinFlow detecting anything in time — not because it adds to the total. Holding the first payment to a payee is the only control that closes the last 4.3%, and it reaches 100% on its own, at more day-to-day friction than either.

A number we deliberately do not lead with. Pair the lockout with containment firing within 24 hours of the first fraudulent payment and the combination reaches 97.7% ($5.72M). We are not claiming that figure, because a 24-hour response is exactly the thing this data cannot establish — there is no timestamp on a dispute or an ops review anywhere in it. It is the upside stated on the containment card, and it belongs there, not in a headline.

Evidence & validation — what the MFA lockout costs real users
# What does an MFA lockout cost real users?
log["failed"] = log.mfa_result.eq("failed")
lg = log.sort_values(["user_id", "login_ts"]).copy()
lg["burst"] = (lg.set_index("login_ts").groupby("user_id")
                 .failed.rolling("60min").sum().to_numpy())
legit = lg[~lg.att_dev]

log.loc[log.failed & ~log.att_dev, "user_id"].nunique()   # 229 of 520 users
(log.failed & ~log.att_dev).sum()                         # 412 failures

legit.burst.max()                                         # 2  <- the worst any real user gets
legit[legit.burst >= 3].user_id.nunique()                 # 0  locked out at threshold 3
legit[legit.burst >= 2].user_id.nunique()                 # 2  locked out at threshold 2

# Real users fumble MFA constantly -- 44% of them have -- but they do it in
# ONES, a median of 12 days apart. Only the attacker fails in bursts.
Evidence & validation — the MFA lockout
# When would a "3 failed MFA in an hour" rule first trip per account?
f = txn[txn.txn_fraud_label]
lg = log.sort_values(["user_id", "login_ts"]).copy()
lg["failed"] = lg.mfa_result.eq("failed")
lg["burst"] = (lg.set_index("login_ts").groupby("user_id")
                 .failed.rolling("60min").sum().to_numpy())
trip = lg[lg.burst >= 3].groupby("user_id").login_ts.min()

# u_0001_01  2026-04-22 20:23     u_0100_01  2026-04-24 03:27
# u_0017_01  2026-04-23 04:58     u_0012_01  2026-04-24 06:21
# u_0101_01  2026-04-23 07:50

stopped = f.apply(lambda r: r.user_id in trip.index
                            and r.txn_ts > trip[r.user_id], axis=1)
f.loc[stopped, "amount"].sum()      # $5,608,619 = 95.7%
f.loc[~stopped]                     # 22 payments, $251,753 still get through

# Those 22 came from sessions entered BEFORE any burst -- at org_0017 the
# attacker's first successful login preceded the MFA hammering entirely.
# So 95.7% is a ceiling, not a guarantee.

How good is FinFlow's process today?

Turned around: of every payment that really was fraud, what verdict did it get? Anything that stops at never reviewed, cleared or low_risk was missed.

Precision 70.4%, recall 44.8%. When ops escalate something they are right seven times in ten — that is a good team. But they only ever reach 45% of the fraud, missing 363 payments worth $3.22M. And it is getting worse, not better: recall was 66.1% on the April wave and 15.3% on the same attacker in June, when 84% of the fraud was never looked at by anyone.

The same word, four different answers

"Precision" depends entirely on which payments you count. Every row below is the raw fraction — how many were really fraud, out of how many carried that verdict.

Recall is the number the review-queue work is about. Of all 658 fraudulent payments, 295 ended up marked high_risk or confirmed_fraud — 295 of 658. The other 363 were cleared, marked low risk, or never opened. Reaching more of them is the goal; changing what goes into the queue is how you get there. Nothing here asks the reviewers to judge differently.

Evidence & validation — precision and recall today
# Turn it around: of every payment that WAS fraud, what did ops call it?
ORDER = ["never reviewed", "cleared", "low_risk", "high_risk", "confirmed_fraud"]

for label, sub in [("all", txn),
                   ("april", txn[txn.txn_ts <  "2026-05-01"]),
                   ("june",  txn[txn.txn_ts >= "2026-06-01"])]:
    fr = sub[sub.txn_fraud_label]
    print(label, fr.ops_review_result.fillna("never reviewed")
                   .value_counts().reindex(ORDER).fillna(0).astype(int).to_dict())

# all   {never reviewed: 321, cleared: 12, low_risk: 30, high_risk: 99, confirmed_fraud: 196}
# april {never reviewed:  90, cleared: 12, low_risk: 28, high_risk: 88, confirmed_fraud: 165}
# june  {never reviewed: 231, cleared:  0, low_risk:  2, high_risk: 11, confirmed_fraud:  31}

esc = txn.ops_review_result.isin(["high_risk", "confirmed_fraud"])
esc.sum()                                     # 419 payments escalated
(esc & txn.txn_fraud_label).sum()             # 295 of them really were fraud

# PRECISION 295/419 = 70.4%   <- when ops escalate, they are usually right
# RECALL    295/658 = 44.8%   <- but they only reach 45% of the fraud

txn.loc[txn.txn_fraud_label & ~esc, "amount"].sum()   # $3,222,956 missed

Speed decides what one wave costs. Containment decides whether there is a second one.

Two halves of the same story, and FinFlow got both wrong. The first half is a race measured in hours; the second is not a race at all.

Half one — the April wave, where hours cost money

Scoped to the April wave only, $3.34M over four days. How much of it is still preventable, against how long FinFlow takes to act after the first fraudulent payment. The second bar is what has already gone by then.

Acting within the first hour keeps 99% of the April money. Waiting three days keeps 23%. The wave ran four days and then stopped on its own, so the entire window to react was measured in hours. That is a genuine speed problem and it cost $3.34M.

Half two — the 60 days of quiet, which is not a speed problem at all

The June wave is usually folded into the same curve. It should not be — nothing about it was fast, and treating it as a slow response lets FinFlow off far too easily.

Between the two waves there were 60 days and zero attacker sessions. The machines that robbed org_0001 in April sat completely idle, then came back on 26 June and walked into three of the same customers for another $2.52M. A block placed on any one of those 60 days would have prevented all of it — there was no race, no alert to catch, nothing to be fast about. FinFlow investigated the April transactions and never blocked the machines that made them. That is not a slow response. It is the absence of one.

The two halves are the same lesson at two speeds. Reacting fast is what limits the damage of the wave you are currently in — worth roughly $40,000 an hour across the 84 hours the April wave ran. Actually closing the incident out, by blocking the machines rather than just refunding the payments, is what stops a second wave existing at all. FinFlow did neither, so it paid twice: $3.34M for being slow, and $2.52M for never finishing.

Evidence & validation
# Replay: a control only gets credit for fraud AFTER it would have fired.
f = txn[txn.txn_fraud_label]
first_fraud = f.txn_ts.min()          # 2026-04-22 22:05

for lag in [0, 24, 48, 72, 168]:
    cut = first_fraud + pd.Timedelta(hours=lag)
    print(lag, f.loc[f.txn_ts > cut, "amount"].sum())

#    0h -> $5,855,739  99.9%
#   24h -> $5,198,392  88.7%
#   48h -> $4,393,737  75.0%
#   72h -> $3,289,058  56.1%
# 1 week -> $2,520,040  43.0%   <- and it never falls below this

# The floor is the June wave. Even a response two months late prevents all
# of it, because the SAME two fingerprints came back on 26 June.

A data-quality finding worth reporting on its own

An obvious control to reach for is "hold payments to a payee added in the last 48 hours". It is not on the list above, because it cannot be built: the column that should say when a payee was added — vendor_add_date — does not. Payee v_0081_022 is an ordinary supplier at org_0081 and demonstrates the whole failure on its own.

Payments to it 445, from 1 April to 29 June
Fraudulent payments to it 0 — nothing suspicious about this payee
vendor_add_date across all 445 rows 2026-06-29 19:55:49 — one single value
Payments dated before that supposed add date 440 of 445
Oldest apparent payee age at payment time −89.7 days

Something edited this payee's record on 29 June, and the field now reports that date for all three months of its history. Age is computed as payment date − add date, so those 440 payments come out negative — and every negative number is less than 48 hours. The rule would freeze 440 payments to a supplier this customer had been paying since April.

Across the whole dataset that is 38,625 payments with the same defect. A 48-hour hold would delay 40,483 legitimate payments rather than the 1,861 it should — 22x worse — and 95% of what it caught would be the bug rather than new payees. vendor_add_date is a last-modified stamp wearing a created-on name. Worth raising with whoever owns the payments data regardless of which controls FinFlow adopts — and it is a good argument for the first item on the list above, which reaches the same fake payees without ever touching this column.

Evidence & validation — the broken date field
# One payee, v_0081_022, tells the whole story.
ex = txn[txn.vendor_id == "v_0081_022"].sort_values("txn_ts")

len(ex)                          # 445 payments, Apr 1 -> Jun 29
ex.vendor_add_date.nunique()     # 1  -- one fixed value on every single row
ex.vendor_add_date.iloc[0]       # 2026-06-29 19:55:49
ex.txn_fraud_label.sum()         # 0  -- a completely ordinary supplier

# 440 of the 445 payments happened BEFORE the date the column claims the
# payee was added:
(ex.txn_ts < ex.vendor_add_date).sum()      # 440

# So "vendor age" for those rows is negative -- as low as -89.7 days -- and
# every negative number is less than 48 hours. A "hold payees under 48h old"
# rule would freeze 440 payments to a supplier with three months of history.

# The field is a LAST-MODIFIED stamp, not a created-on date. Something
# touched this vendor record on 29 June and rewrote its history.
Evidence & validation
age_h = (txn.txn_ts - txn.vendor_add_date).dt.total_seconds() / 3600

# Honest version -- exclude the rows where the field is broken
hold = age_h.between(0, 48)
txn.loc[hold & txn.txn_fraud_label, "amount"].sum()   # $2,981,069 = 50.9%
(hold & ~txn.txn_fraud_label).sum()                   # 1,861 legitimate payments held

# Naive version -- what you would actually get if you shipped it today
(age_h < 0).sum()                                     # 38,625 rows dated AFTER their payment
((age_h < 48) & ~txn.txn_fraud_label).sum()           # 40,483 legitimate payments held

# 22x worse, entirely because vendor_add_date is not what its name says.
# This control is not a risk decision yet. It is a data-quality prerequisite.

Honest limits on these numbers

Worth saying before anyone acts on them.

Every "would have prevented" figure assumes someone noticed. This dataset has no timestamp on a dispute or an ops review — only on payments and logins — so we cannot tell when FinFlow learned about the April wave. That makes any "if they had reacted within N hours" number a statement about what a control is worth, not about what FinFlow could have achieved with what it knew. The one figure that escapes this is cross-customer containment's: it needs only that FinFlow knew at some point before 26 June, which is provable from the 165 April payments ops marked confirmed_fraud.

These are retrospective percentages against one campaign. They say what would have stopped this attacker, not the next one. A different crew that avoids offshore banks, or spaces payments out over weeks, defeats the MFA lockout's 60-minute window, and the narrowed hold variants that lean on a foreign bank or a wire, entirely.

Cross-customer containment is safe only because it fires after a breach is confirmed. Do not extend it into "any device at two customers is suspicious" — this dataset cannot tell you what that would cost, because 726 of its 728 devices serve exactly one customer and 724 serve exactly one user. It contains no legitimate device sharing at all, so it has nothing to say about the bookkeepers and outsourced finance teams who really do work across several customers from one laptop.

The review-queue model's headline is inflated by the data. It reaches 100% of the June wave, but the fraud here separates far more cleanly than real fraud does. Treat the 9-alerts-a-day figure as an upper bound — and note the recommendation does not depend on it, since the June slots were already sufficient.

The 100% for holding first payments assumes the attacker always adds a new payee. It was, here. An attacker who instead hijacks an existing vendor the customer already pays — changing its bank details rather than adding a payee — produces no first payment and walks straight past it. That is a real pattern, and it is why the is_new_bank_account condition is worth keeping in some form.

Evidence & validation — the review-queue work
j = txn[txn.txn_ts >= "2026-06-01"]
jrev = j.ops_review_result.notna()

jrev.sum()                                  # 652 review slots used in June
j.txn_fraud_label.sum()                     # 275 fraudulent payments
(jrev & j.txn_fraud_label).sum()            # 44 of them were opened
(jrev & ~j.txn_fraud_label).sum()           # 608 slots spent on clean payments

# The 275 would have fitted in the 652 slots with 377 to spare.
# Capacity was never the problem.
Evidence & validation
# What ops does today
txn.ops_review_result.notna().mean()                       # 1.17% of payments
(txn.ops_review_result.isin(["high_risk", "confirmed_fraud"])
 & txn.txn_fraud_label).sum()                              # 295 of 658 = 44.8%

(txn.ops_review_result.eq("cleared") & txn.txn_fraud_label).sum()   # 12 cleared as fine
(txn.ops_review_result.isna()       & txn.txn_fraud_label).sum()    # 321 never seen

# Model trained on Apr-May, tested on the unseen June wave:
#   275 alerts  ->  275/275 June fraud caught
#   = 9.2 alerts/day, against roughly 24/day of existing capacity
# The constraint is not headcount. It is which 1.2% they look at.

The gap this has to close

FinFlow's review process is precise but not thorough. That points at one number.

Recall is the target. Precision is not the constraint and should not be spent casually — the gap to close is the fraud nobody ever looks at. And because review capacity is fixed, raising recall means better selection, not more alerts. That is what the stack below is for.

Score the session, not just the payment

One design choice matters more than the model. Both framings work; they are not equivalent. Trained on April–May, tested on the unseen June wave.

48 sessions produced all 275 fraudulent June payments. Scoring sessions means 5.7x fewer things to review for the same money — and a session flagged at login can be stopped before a payment exists. Payment scoring is still needed as a second net, but the session is the cheaper place to intervene.

Evidence & validation — session vs payment
# Same features, same time split, two different things to score.
CUT = pd.Timestamp("2026-06-01")     # train on Apr-May, test on the June wave

# A: one row per PAYMENT      B: one row per LOGIN SESSION
#    positives 275/60,473        positives 48/23,692
#    PR-AUC 1.000                PR-AUC 0.996

# Alerts a day needed to reach every fraudulent item in June:
#    payment-level  -> 10/day
#    session-level  ->  3/day

jf = txn[(txn.txn_ts >= CUT) & txn.txn_fraud_label]
len(jf)                      # 275 fraudulent payments
jf.session_id.nunique()      # 48 sessions produced all of them

# 5.7x fewer things to review for the same money -- and a session can be
# stopped before any payment exists.

These features already work — here they are, tested

Before proposing features in the abstract, here are four of them run against the real data. Each is computed from behaviour alone — none reads txn_fraud_label. Scored across all 110 customers they isolate the five that were robbed, exactly. This is also how the investigation fixed its own boundary without leaning on the label.

Methodology

Four indicators, each computed from behaviour alone. An org scores one point per indicator it trips; the alert threshold is 3 of 4. The right-hand column shows how each indicator performs on its own — which is why the score combines them.

#IndicatorRuleWhy On its own
1Failed-MFA country spread mfa_fail_countries >= 3 A real user fumbles MFA from one place. Rotating IPs is an attacker. 5/5 victims
+1 false: org_0068
2Cross-org device shared_device_sessions > 0 Users and vendors are namespaced per org — a device fingerprint is the only object that can cross an org boundary. 5/5 victims
no false positives
3Payments to brand-new payees burner_vendor_pays >= 5 Payees with almost no history, foreign bank, bank details days old — exactly what the attacker's fake payees looked like. 5/5 victims
+1 false: org_0056
4Foreign login new for that user new_foreign_cc_max_user >= 3 Not "foreign" — foreign and unprecedented for this specific user, counted per user. A company with staff abroad has employees who are always in the same country; a hijacked account is suddenly everywhere. 5/5 victims
+3 false

No indicator is clean on its own except #2, and each carries a different false positive — org_0068 for #1, org_0056 for #3, and org_0009/0026/0042 for #4 — so combining them cancels every one. Measuring #4 per user rather than counting foreign logins outright is what produced the gap below: the score went from a continuous spread to two clusters with nothing between them.

Confirmed victim No fraud Each square is one organization, ranked by score.

Five organizations score 4 of 4. Everything else scores 1 or 0 — nothing lands on 2 or 3. 100 of 110 orgs score zero. Because the gap is total, the cut-off is not a judgement call: any threshold from 2 to 4 returns the same five orgs, and they are exactly the five confirmed victims. So "could there be a sixth victim nobody adjudicated?" has an answer — no, not on any behaviour visible in this data.

FinFlow's own reviewers agree, independently. ops_review_result = confirmed_fraud appears in exactly these five organizations and nowhere else — 196 payments, all inside the boundary. That is a second, human source landing on the same five. But note high_risk is far noisier: it appears in 61 orgs, and 115 of its 223 uses sit in orgs with no fraud at all. Ops' conclusions are clean; ops' suspicions are not.

Honest limitation: the code below reads no labels, but I chose these four indicators after studying the attack. So this is not an out-of-sample discovery — the correct claim is "having characterised the attack, a label-free test sweeps all 110 orgs and nothing outside the five matches." The threshold is no longer a judgement call — with indicator 4 measured per user no org scores 2 or 3, so anything from 2 to 4 gives the same five. (With a plain "20+ foreign logins" rule it was a call: at 2 of 4, org_0068 came along.) The remaining caveat is indicator 2: cross-org device reuse is partly an artifact of synthetic data — real bookkeepers and MSPs share devices across clients, so it would not stay clean in production.

Evidence & validation
# Score all 110 orgs on indicators that never touch txn_fraud_label.
log = log.sort_values("login_ts")
idx = sorted(txn.org_id.unique())
sweep = pd.DataFrame(index=idx)

# 1. failed-MFA country spread -- real users fumble MFA from one place
fm = log[log.mfa_result.eq("failed")]
sweep["mfa_fail_countries"] = (fm.groupby("org_id").ip_country
                                 .nunique().reindex(idx).fillna(0))

# 2. a device seen at more than one org
dev_orgs = log.groupby("device_id").org_id.nunique()
shared = set(dev_orgs[dev_orgs > 1].index)
sweep["shared_device_sessions"] = (log[log.device_id.isin(shared)]
                                   .groupby("org_id").size().reindex(idx).fillna(0))

# 3. burner vendors -- no history, foreign bank, fresh bank details
vcount = txn.groupby("vendor_id").size()
burner = set(vcount[vcount <= 6].index)
sweep["burner_vendor_pays"] = (txn[txn.vendor_id.isin(burner)
                                   & txn.vendor_bank_country.ne("US")
                                   & txn.is_new_bank_account]
                               .groupby("org_id").size().reindex(idx).fillna(0))

# 4. foreign AND new for that user, counted per user (derived below)
log["foreign_new"] = (~log.duplicated(["user_id", "ip_country"], keep="first")
                      & log.ip_country.ne("US"))
sweep["new_foreign_cc_max_user"] = (log[log.foreign_new]
                                    .groupby(["org_id", "user_id"]).ip_country.nunique()
                                    .groupby("org_id").max().reindex(idx).fillna(0))

sweep["score"] = ((sweep.mfa_fail_countries      >= 3).astype(int)
                + (sweep.shared_device_sessions  >  0).astype(int)
                + (sweep.burner_vendor_pays      >= 5).astype(int)
                + (sweep.new_foreign_cc_max_user >= 3).astype(int))

sweep.score.value_counts().sort_index()
# 0 -> 100 orgs | 1 -> 5 | 2 -> 0 | 3 -> 0 | 4 -> 5

sorted(sweep[sweep.score >= 3].index) == sorted(VICTIMS)   # True

# --- indicator 4: "foreign" is the wrong question ---
log["foreign_new"] = (~log.duplicated(["user_id", "ip_country"], keep="first")
                      & log.ip_country.ne("US"))

# count NEW foreign countries per user, then take the worst user in each org
(log[log.foreign_new].groupby(["org_id", "user_id"]).ip_country.nunique()
    .groupby("org_id").max())

# org_0068  1   <- HK employee is always in HK, IN employee always in IN
# org_0017  4   <- one account suddenly appearing from four new countries

# --- each indicator on its own ---
# cross-org device        -> 5 orgs, 5/5 victims, 0 false positives
# mfa_fail_countries>=3   -> 6 orgs, 5/5 victims, 1 false (org_0068)
# burner_vendor_pays>=5   -> 6 orgs, 5/5 victims, 1 false (org_0056)
# new_foreign_cc>=3       -> 8 orgs, 5/5 victims, 3 false
# (the naive foreign>=20  -> 9 orgs, 3/5 victims, 6 false -- replaced)

# --- combined: the scores split into two clusters with a hole between ---
sweep.score.value_counts().sort_index()
# 0 -> 100 orgs | 1 -> 5 | 2 -> 0 | 3 -> 0 | 4 -> 5
# Any threshold in 2..4 returns the same five orgs.

# --- corroboration from a completely different source ---
ops = txn.assign(r=txn.ops_review_result.fillna("not_reviewed"))
sorted(ops[ops.r.eq("confirmed_fraud")].org_id.unique()) == sorted(VICTIMS)   # True

(ops.r.eq("high_risk").groupby(ops.org_id).any()).sum()      # 61 orgs
ops[ops.r.eq("high_risk") & ~ops.org_id.isin(VICTIMS)].shape[0]   # 115 of 223

# Ops' CONCLUSIONS land on the same five. Ops' SUSPICIONS are spread
# across 61 orgs, over half of them in orgs with no fraud at all.

The near miss: proof the features discriminate

org_0068 has 454 foreign login sessions — more than every victim combined — and zero fraud. If the test couldn't tell it apart, the boundary would be luck rather than evidence.

org_0068 is a distributed company, not a breach. One employee always logs in from Hong Kong, another always from India — on their own devices, paying US vendors. 0 of its 454 foreign sessions are new for that user, and its worst user has appeared from just 1 new foreign country. At org_0017 all 17 foreign sessions are new, from 4 new countries on a single account. The discriminator isn't "foreign", it's "foreign and new for this user" — which is why a plain country rule would bury ops in false positives.

Evidence & validation
# org_0068 looks foreign. Is it compromised?
o = log[log.org_id == "org_0068"]
homes = o.groupby("user_id").ip_country.agg(lambda s: s.mode()[0])
# u_0068_01 US | u_0068_02 US | u_0068_03 HK | u_0068_04 IN

# Count foreign logins that are NEW for that particular user
sum(1 for u, c in zip(o.user_id, o.ip_country) if c != "US" and c != homes[u])
# 0        <- all 454 foreign sessions are each user's own home country

# Same calculation on a real victim:
# org_0017 -> 17 foreign sessions, ALL 17 new for that user

# The signal is not "foreign". It is "foreign, and new for this user."

Tier 1 — Rules, for the things that are not probability questions

Five specific checks, each with the threshold, the alert volume it would generate, and the moment in this incident it would have fired. Precision is the share of alerts that turned out to sit on fraud.

RuleAlertsPrecisionWhat it would have caught here
R1 Block a device confirmed malicious at one customer, across all customers. Not "seen at two customers" — only after a breach is confirmed. 1.5/day86% d_5019b1fc56a9 was confirmed at org_0001 in April and was still logging into org_0100 and org_0101 on 26 June. Blocking it in April prevents the entire second wave — $2.52M.

Read the two numbers to the left carefully. They are measured on the broader trigger — a device seen at a second customer — because that is what can be replayed over 90 days of log data. In this dataset the two coincide: only 2 of 728 devices ever cross an org boundary and both are the attacker's. The rule as written above fires strictly less often, since it also waits for a confirmed breach. Treat 1.5/day as a ceiling on the alert volume, and see the limits card — the broad version is not the one to ship.
R2 Lock the account after 3 failed MFA challenges within 60 minutes. 0.5/day14% u_0001_01 took 21 failed challenges between 20:20 and 21:11 on 22 April. First fraudulent payment: 22:05. The rule trips at 20:23 — 102 minutes early. It fires on exactly five accounts in 90 days, and all five are victims.
R3 Flag a successful login from a different country within 6 hours of the previous one. 2.8/day33% u_0001_01 on 23 April: 01:30 PH → 01:55 SG → 02:22 US → 03:03 SG → 03:32 PH → 03:51 VN → 04:38 US. Seven countries in three hours.
R4 Flag a login from a country this specific user has never used. Not "foreign" — new for them. 0.6/day9% u_0017_01 had 65 consecutive sessions from US/Arizona, then SG, HK, VN and PH inside four days. Weakest rule alone, but it is what separates a hijacked account from a company with staff abroad.
R5 Hold the first-ever payment from a customer to a payee, pending a second approver. 31/day13% Every one of the attacker's 362 fake payees had a first payment. Holding it stops the payee being used at all, so the 296 follow-on payments never happen either. The highest-friction rule here by far.
Evidence & validation — the five rules replayed
# Every rule below replayed over the 90 days. "Fires" counts sessions;
# precision is the share of those that produced fraudulent payments.

# R1  a device already seen at another customer (running set, not hindsight)
seen, flag = {}, []
for dev, org in zip(log.device_id, log.org_id):
    s = seen.setdefault(dev, set()); s.add(org)
    flag.append(len(s) > 1)
#   136 sessions, 1.5/day, 86% precision

# R2  three or more failed MFA for one account inside 60 minutes
lg = log.sort_values(["user_id", "login_ts"]).copy()
lg["failed"] = lg.mfa_result.eq("failed")
lg["burst"] = (lg.set_index("login_ts").groupby("user_id")
                 .failed.rolling("60min").sum().to_numpy())
#   42 sessions, 0.5/day -- fires on 5 accounts, all of them victims

# R3  successful login from a different country within 6 hours of the last
#   254 sessions, 2.8/day, 33% precision

# R4  a country this specific user has never logged in from
#   54 sessions, 0.6/day, 9% precision -- weakest alone, useful combined

# R5  first-ever payment from a customer to a payee
txn.groupby(["org_id", "vendor_id"]).txn_ts.min()
#   2,820 over 90 days = 31/day; 362 of them were the attacker's fake payees

Tier 2 — A model, ranking everything ambiguous

This is the queue-ordering layer, and the thing that actually moves recall. Three realistic candidates.

CandidateForAgainst
Logistic regression A coefficient is a sentence — it survives a customer dispute, a regulator and a review panel. Stable when positives are scarce, which in fraud they always are. Calibrated probabilities, which matters when the threshold is set by review capacity. Retrains in seconds, so you can retrain often. Learns no interactions unless you build them as columns. Fraud is usually a combination, so that work lands on you.
Random forest Finds interactions for free. Robust to outliers and mixed scales, minimal preprocessing, short path to a first version. Feature importance misleads when features are correlated — and fraud features always are. Probabilities need calibrating before you can threshold. "300 trees voted" is not an explanation you can give a customer whose payment you held.
Gradient boosting Usually the strongest on tabular data. Handles missing values natively, which is a real advantage when review outcomes are sparse by design. The most hyperparameters, so the most ways to overfit and the most temptation to stop thinking. Hardest to explain. Most likely to quietly exploit a leaky feature.

Sequence: ship logistic regression first, with hand-built combination features. Run the other two alongside as benchmarks. A wide gap means interactions matter — build them explicitly or accept the complexity. A narrow gap means keep the simple one.

Tier 3 — Worth considering: ensembles, unsupervised, neural

Tiers 1 and 2 detect fraud that has already been labelled. This tier is for the attacks nobody has catalogued yet, and for the last of the recall gap.

Inference cost is not the constraint here. Even at several times peak, nothing in this problem is compute-bound — you could run an ensemble of five models and an autoencoder on every session and never notice. The real constraints are explainability, maintenance and label scarcity, so heavier methods should be judged on those rather than on latency.

Ensembles

Blend models that fail differently. A linear model, a tree ensemble and an unsupervised anomaly score make different mistakes, and combining their scores usually beats any one of them.

For: near-free accuracy at this volume. Degrades gracefully — if one component drifts, the others hold. Lets you keep an explainable model in the mix rather than choosing between accuracy and explanation.
Against: you now maintain several models and a combiner. Though "flagged by 3 of 4 detectors" is often more intuitive for ops than a single probability. Stacking on scarce positives overfits easily — keep the combiner simple, a weighted average or a logistic regression over the component scores.

Unsupervised

Autoencoder reconstruction error, isolation forests, or per-customer behavioural baselines. All ask the same question: is this unlike how this customer normally operates?

Why it matters: it needs no labels, so it is not limited to campaigns already in the training set. That is the entire argument for including it — everything else here can only find what has been seen before.
Against: anomaly is not fraud. A customer's genuine first international wire is a large anomaly. Expect poor standalone precision, and use it two ways: as a feature into the ensemble, and as a small human-reviewed discovery queue for spotting patterns you have no feature for yet.

Neural networks

Worth considering precisely because inference is free — but only for what they are genuinely better at.

Sequence models A session is an ordered event stream: login → add payee → payment → payment. RNNs and transformers model that ordering directly, where engineered aggregates flatten it away. This is where a network earns its place.
Entity embeddings Learned representations for devices, payees and customers — capturing "similar to known bad" without hand-built graph features.
Autoencoders The anomaly component above, for the unsupervised tier.

Against: hungry for positives, which fraud never has. Hardest to explain to a declined customer. Most likely to memorise an artifact. Do not reach for a network until the engineered features and the ensemble have plateaued — and if one wins big on a few hundred positives, suspect leakage before celebrating.

Ordering: ship Tiers 1 and 2. Add the unsupervised score as a feature and a discovery queue. Then ensemble. Neural methods last, and only if sequence structure is demonstrably where the remaining signal lives.

The features worth building

Named, with what each computes and what it looked like during this incident. The last column flags where a Tier 1 rule already covers the same ground — see the note below, because the answer is not simply "drop it".

FeatureWhat it computesIn this incident Rule overlap
amount_over_org_median Payment ÷ this customer's own running median payment. Fraud runs at 1.8x the customer's usual against 1.0x for clean traffic — real separation, but modest. Worth having because the raw amount is useless: 294 legitimate payments are larger than the biggest fraudulent one. none
payments_this_session Running count of payments already made in this login session. Attack sessions carry a median of 5, normal sessions 2. The busiest pushed 9 payments in 87 minutes. none
new_payees_added_24h Payees this customer has added in the last day. org_0017 gained 24 fake payees in four days, against a normal rate of about 0.5 a day. none
hours_since_user_first_used_device Derived from login_ts, not from the shipped is_new_device column. The shipped column contradicts itself — it flags a device as new after two successful sessions on it. Derive your own. none
new_payee_new_bank_foreign_wire All four conditions at once. A linear model cannot learn interactions, so the ones you believe in have to become columns. Fires 324 times in 90 days and 85.5% are fraud — far sharper than any of the four alone. partial (R5 covers one of the four)
failed_mfa_60m Count of failed MFA challenges for this user in the trailing hour. Peaks at 21. Never above 2 for any legitimate user. R2 — keep the count
country_new_for_user First time this specific user has logged in from this country. u_0017_01: 65 consecutive US sessions, then SG. org_0068's Hong Kong employee never trips it. R4
orgs_touched_by_device Running count of distinct customers this machine has been seen at. Never exceeds 1 for 726 of 728 devices. R1
first_payment_to_payee Has this customer ever paid this payee before. All 362 fake payees had one. Fires 31 times a day. R5

On the overlap: keep the measurement, never the verdict. Feeding a rule's boolean output into the model is genuine double-counting — the model just relearns the rule and you lose the ability to tell them apart. But the underlying continuous measure carries signal the rule cannot see, because a rule is a threshold. failed_mfa_60m is the clearest case: R2 fires at 3 or more, and 549 sessions sit at 1 or 2 — invisible to the rule, not zero to the model.

One consequence to design around. If a Tier 1 rule blocks a session, that session never reaches the model — so the model trains only on what the rules let through. Any rule-overlapping feature will therefore look weaker to the model than it really is, because its strongest cases were removed upstream. That is expected and fine, but it means you cannot judge those features by their model coefficients, and you must evaluate the stack end to end rather than the model alone.

One to avoid: org_id as a feature. With 110 levels the model would learn which customers were attacked, which is the definition of not generalising. Same caution for raw country dummies — "new for this user" carries the signal, "is it Vietnam" does not.

One that cannot be built yet: payee age. The obvious hours_since_payee_added is unusable because vendor_add_date is a last-modified stamp — 21% of payments predate their own payee's creation date.

Point-in-time discipline, always. Every feature must be computable from data available at the moment of scoring. This is the easiest way to build something that looks excellent and fails in production — it happened once here: a cross-customer device feature computed over the whole window reported perfect precision until it was rebuilt to count only what was known so far.

Evidence & validation — the features, computed
# Every feature is computed from rows at or before the moment being scored.

# --- how unusual is this payment for THIS customer ---
med = txn.groupby("org_id").amount.transform(
          lambda s: s.shift().expanding().median())      # prior rows only
txn["amount_over_org_median"] = txn.amount / med
#   fraud 1.8x the customer's own running median; clean 1.0x
#   a real gap but a modest one -- amount is a weak signal here

txn["payments_this_session"] = txn.groupby("session_id").cumcount()
#   attack sessions: median 5 payments | normal: 2 | busiest: 9 in 87 minutes

# --- the overlap question, settled by looking ---
lg = log.sort_values(["user_id", "login_ts"]).copy()
lg["failed"] = lg.mfa_result.eq("failed")
lg["failed_mfa_60m"] = (lg.set_index("login_ts").groupby("user_id")
                          .failed.rolling("60min").sum().to_numpy())

lg.failed_mfa_60m.value_counts().sort_index()
#   0 -> 72,030 | 1 -> 541 | 2 -> 8 | 3 -> 5 | 4 -> 7 | 5 -> 5

# Rule R2 fires at >= 3. That leaves 549 sessions at 1 or 2 that no rule ever
# sees, and whose value is not zero. Keep the COUNT as a feature; never feed
# the rule's own boolean verdict, or the model just relearns the rule.

# --- entity graph, as a running count ---
seen, orgs_so_far = {}, []
for dev, org in zip(log.device_id, log.org_id):
    s = seen.setdefault(dev, set()); s.add(org)
    orgs_so_far.append(len(s))
log["orgs_touched_by_device"] = orgs_so_far          # never > 1 for 726 of 728

# --- the interaction, spelled out because a linear model cannot learn it ---
txn["new_payee_new_bank_foreign_wire"] = (
      (~txn.duplicated(["org_id", "vendor_id"], keep="first"))
    & txn.is_new_bank_account
    & txn.vendor_bank_country.ne("US")
    & txn.transfer_type.isin(["wire", "international wire"]))
#   fires 324 times in 90 days, 85.5% of them fraud

Evaluation, and living with it in production

PR-AUC and recall-at-k Never ROC-AUC. At sub-1% base rates it flatters everything — every model tried here scored above 0.96 on ROC.
Split by time, never at random A random split lets the model see the future.
The threshold is an ops decision Set by how many alerts a day the team will genuinely work, then report recall and precision at that point. A model evaluated at 0.5 tells you nothing useful.
Measure dollars, not just counts Recall on value is what the business feels.

Three production realities to design for now.
Labels arrive late and incomplete. Disputes lag weeks and some fraud is never reported at all, so recent data always looks cleaner than it is. Never evaluate on the most recent window, and expect the training set to under-count fraud permanently.

Attackers adapt; the model does not. Anything trained on last quarter degrades against next quarter. Plan retraining cadence and drift monitoring up front, and watch the fire rate of every rule and feature — a signal that suddenly stops firing usually means evasion, not success.

Time-to-detection is currently unmeasurable. There is no timestamp on a dispute or a review anywhere in this data. That is the number a risk team should manage against, and fixing the instrumentation is probably worth more than any model improvement on this list.

AI-usage logthe required deliverable, live

AI-Usage Log

1. Researching and understanding the problem

  • Extracted the text from FinFlow_Candidate_Brief.pdf and had it summarise the setup, the three label fields and the deliverables.
  • Had it profile the two CSVs before I formed any hypothesis: shapes, dtypes, null counts, cardinality, and whether the session_id join actually holds.
  • Used it as a sounding board on the label semantics — what dispute_flag, ops_review_result and txn_fraud_label each mean and when each becomes available. That conversation is what produced the leakage rules I worked under.
  • Asked it to check my own hypotheses rather than confirm them. When I suggested the attacker's device might belong to a shared bookkeeper serving all five customers, it tested and disproved it — the devices have zero history before 22 April.

Danny:     

2. Data processing, coding, and model building

  • Standing instructions before any code. Wrote CLAUDE.md first: the 4-hour cap, the leakage rules, time-based splits, fixed seeds, notebook runs top to bottom. Then had it build analysis.ipynb section by section at my pace, rather than hand me a finished file I had not watched being made.
  • Point-in-time features only. New device, new country, MFA-failure counts, running device-to-customer counts and expanding per-customer medians, every one derived from login_ts so nothing uses information that did not exist when the payment was submitted.
  • Join integrity as assert, not print, so a broken join stops the notebook instead of quietly producing a wrong number. session_id is the key: 0 payments without a session, 1,944 sessions (2.7%) without a payment, and a validate="m:1" merge returning exactly 184,432 rows. The same checking turned up a limit worth knowing — no payment ever lands more than 99 minutes after its login, so sessions here are capped in a way real AP sessions are not, which bounds anything session-scoped.
  • Compared two model framings — score the payment, or score the login session — on a time-based split, with ablations to show which features were actually load-bearing.
  • The sharpest finding came from a chart, not a model. Rebuilding the break-in timeline around episodes showed June was not a break-in at all: zero failed MFA challenges across the three repeat-victim accounts, against 46 in April. So the MFA lockout cannot fire on the second wave; it prevents that money only by locking the account back in April. A real qualification on its 95.7%, and I only found it by asking why a chart showed one episode when three customers were hit twice.

Danny:     

3. Verifying AI output

  • Any number that could reach a slide is recomputed a second way before it counts.
  • Join sanity every time: row counts before/after, orphans, user/org consistency.
  • I built a harness that executes every code block on the dashboard against the real CSVs and compares the values in its comments to what actually runs. Current state: 80/80 values verified, 24/24 blocks executable.
  • Audited the published dashboard end to end against the CSVs, recomputing every headline from scratch — the payment and session counts, the $5.86M, the five victim orgs, precision and recall, the four-indicator sweep. All reproduced. Every defect it turned up sat in the prose or the chart maths, never in the analysis underneath.

produced a confident, plausible, wrong answer.

is wrong. Reading for sense catches the other, where the arithmetic is fine and the sentence sitting on top of it is not. So the checking ran three ways.

  • Independent investigation, then reconciliation — early on, while I was still deciding what was true. I worked the data myself alongside it and compared conclusions, rather than take its first pass as the starting point.
  • Delegation with sampled query checks — once we had agreed on the picture. It led; I pulled queries at intervals and ran them myself.
  • A standing read-for-sense pass over everything it produced, asking one question of every claim: does this sentence match what the code actually establishes?

reading rather than recomputing:

  • “Isn't there 2 break-ins?” The chart was anchored on the first episode. Chasing that surfaced that June was not a break-in at all — zero failed MFA challenges against 46 in April — a real qualification on the lockout's 95.7% that nothing else had caught.
  • “MFA passing in June is expected if the device is familiar.” It had written that the April credentials still worked, asserting a cause this data does not record. An over-claim, not a wrong number.
  • “So a login attempt on that device but not a fraud session is marked as deterred?” The comment said "blocked." The code said "did not move money." Both were true, but the code had not earned the word.
  • “Is 'I' Danny or Claude?” Two rows had the attribution backwards, crediting me with work it had done.

Every one is the same shape: the computation was correct and the sentence describing it was not. Recomputation would not have caught any of them, because the numbers were real.

Where the AI was wrong
What happenedA feature that leaked the future. "Device seen at more than one customer" was computed over all 90 days, so it knew a device would later appear elsewhere. Reported 100% recall at 100% precision.
How it was caughtThe perfect score is what made me look. At the moment of the first fraudulent payment that device had only been seen at one customer — the rule could not have fired.
OutcomeRebuilt as a forward pass. Recall fell to 95.4%.

Nine other defects were caught and fixed the same way. Among them: an MFA-burst feature that returned exactly 0% recall, which proved to be an index-alignment bug rather than a dead signal; a headline that used a conditional-upside figure as if it were the baseline; a chart that offered a circular row as evidence; and an over-claim about credential rotation that I caught in conversation.

Where I disagreed and was right
What I pushed back onI suggested "foreign and new for that user" instead of a plain foreign-login count.
What changedIt replaced the weaker indicator. The org-level score went from a continuous spread to two clusters with nothing between them — 100 customers at zero, five at four — so the alert threshold stopped being a judgement call.

Four other pushbacks changed the deliverable, the largest being the cross-customer headline: I asked how FinFlow could have known on 22 April when the customer's report came later, and with no dispute or review timestamp anywhere in the data it dropped from $5.20M to the $2.52M that survives the question.
